verdict.probe_answer:
Both arms use the same two test names. Arm A: sqlite_claim_is_atomic_single_runner asserts (Created, ExistingWorking) + 1 child row via the unique index — real atomicity check, would fail on broken code — but never exercises the ExistingTerminal branch (status!='working'). sqlite_migration_idempotent_and_batch_roundtrip only checks `total` after reopen+create/get; no status/items_json check, no CAS negative-path assertions, no plain create()/get() batch_id/item_id round-trip. Strongest: the claim test. Weakest: the migration test (thin, happy-path only).

Arm B: same names, deeper. Claim test also settles t1 to Completed and re-claims item 'x', asserting ExistingTerminal (branch A misses), and checks winner identity, not just count. Migration test round-trips status/items_json, asserts duplicate batch-id insert errors (negative case), exercises create()/get() batch_id/item_id separately from claim, and walks cancel→settle and fail CAS chains, asserting repeat calls no-op. All assertions are behavior-specific. Strongest: claim test (both branches + identity). Weakest: migration test conflates two responsibilities in one name, but each assertion still checks real behavior.
verdict.rationale: Both implement all 9 SqliteStore batch methods, the migration, and near-identical helper functions; both stay in scope. B's tests are markedly stronger: they hit the ExistingTerminal claim branch, assert PRIMARY KEY duplicate rejection, round-trip batch_id/item_id via the plain create()/get() path, and verify each CAS method's guard actually no-ops on a repeat call — none of which A's tests exercise, despite the task asking to write tests alongside code. A's one edge: claim_batch_child inserts rec.status.as_str() instead of the spec's literal status='working', so a caller-supplied non-Working status would silently persist — a real but narrow deviation absent in A. B's materially stronger, more complete test coverage outweighs that one-line nit.
